original_question: In two dimensions, consider elastic materials built from one elastic phase and void, and impose the limiting incompressible/auxetic condition kappa*=0 together with 1/kappa=0 for the solid phase. Is 4 mu / 5 the largest possible effective shear modulus mu* under these constraints?
target_in_paper: Section 4, Problem 4.4: "Is 4μ/5 the largest possible value of μ∗ for a two-dimensional elastic material with voids, given that κ∗ = 1/κ = 0?" ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the core of Problem 4.4: the two-dimensional setting, a material built from one elastic phase and void, the exact constraints κ∗ = 0 and 1/κ = 0, and the candidate extremal value 4μ/5 for the effective shear modulus μ∗. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))
missing_details: The paper’s setup is specifically an isotropic elastic solid phase with bulk modulus κ and shear modulus μ mixed with void; your draft says only “one elastic phase and void,” which omits the isotropy and the meaning of κ and μ. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))

The moduli κ∗ and μ∗ are the effective bulk and effective shear moduli of the composite, so the question is implicitly about two-dimensional composites whose effective response is isotropic; otherwise the pair (κ∗, μ∗) is not the right stand-alone parametrization. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))

The optimization is over all admissible two-dimensional microgeometries/composites with voids; the refined question should make the quantifier explicit by asking whether μ∗ can ever exceed 4μ/5, or equivalently whether 4μ/5 is the supremum. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))

The paper motivates the problem through the “ultimate auxetic material” discussion, but the official statement uses the exact equalities κ∗ = 0 and 1/κ = 0, not merely a limiting or approximate auxetic regime. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))

The appearance of 4μ/5 is not arbitrary: it comes from the candidate construction leading to equation (4.5), namely 1/μ∗ = 5/(4μ) + 1/(4κ), followed by the stated invariance argument that allows one to assume 1/κ = 0 without loss of generality. A stand-alone formulation should preserve that origin in the background, even if the question itself stays at Problem 4.4. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))

No ambient ring/field, polynomial degree, homogeneity, nilpotency condition, operator-algebra setup, or “for all sufficiently large m” quantifier is part of this problem; it is a continuum effective-moduli question in elasticity, so those items are inapplicable here and should not be imported. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))
refined_question: Among all two-dimensional composites made from void and a single isotropic elastic phase with bulk modulus κ and shear modulus μ, whose effective response is isotropic with effective bulk modulus κ∗ and effective shear modulus μ∗, and under the exact constraints that the solid phase is incompressible (1/κ = 0) and the composite satisfies κ∗ = 0, is the largest possible effective shear modulus equal to 4μ/5? ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))
justification: This draft is targeting Section 4’s “ultimate auxetic material” problem, not the quasi-convexification problems from Section 2. Section 4 first introduces the effective pair (κ∗, μ∗) for isotropic composites of one elastic phase (with bulk modulus κ and shear modulus μ) and void, then Problem 4.3 asks for microstructures maximizing μ∗ − cκ∗; when c is very large, the paper explains that this points toward maximizing μ∗ under very small κ∗. The next paragraphs build a two-dimensional candidate construction, derive equation (4.5), and then, using the stated invariance, reduce to the incompressible-solid case 1/κ = 0, where the candidate value becomes μ∗ = 4μ/5. Problem 4.4 is exactly the sharpened official question your draft is trying to capture. ([par.nsf.gov](https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10232880))
